title: The Bean and the Red Cell
endLine: A red cell's antioxidant defense leans on NADPH, gated by G6PD.

scenes.tts: Last time, glutathione took the oxidant hits, and NADPH from this pathway recharged it. So why can a plate of fava beans destroy someone's red blood cells?
scenes.narration: Last time, glutathione took the oxidant hits, and NADPH from this pathway recharged it. So why can a plate of fava beans destroy someone's red blood cells?
scenes.caption: Last time, glutathione took the oxidant hits, and NADPH from this pathway recharged it. So why can a plate of fava beans destroy someone's red blood cells?
scenes.visual: Carry the first film's colour map: YELLOW = glucose-6-phosphate and sugars; ORANGE = the pentose phosphate pathway and its enzyme G6PD; PURPLE = NADPH; TEAL = glutathione (GSH / GSSG); RED = reactive oxygen (8-pointed RED stars, as in the first film) and damage; GREY = enzyme names and de-emphasized things; white dots = electrons. New in this film: the red blood cell itself, a soft ROSE outline (#E8A0A8, clearly lighter and pinker than the damage RED) with small ROSE hemoglobin dots inside. ONE WORLD for the whole film: a single cut-away red blood cell, a flattened disc seen face-on, filling about 65% of the frame height, centre-left; blood plasma around it with slow drifting particles. A small 'schematic' tag sits bottom right all film. During the link-back sentence, the first film's glutathione loop fades in inside the cell, rebuilt in the same form: a TEAL chip '2 GSH' at left, a TEAL chip 'GSSG' at right, a TEAL arrow across the top (a RED star hits it and GSH becomes GSSG) and a TEAL arrow back along the bottom, driven by PURPLE NADPH dots carrying white electron dots. On 'fava beans', a plate of three plain olive-brown bean icons (not GREEN; no structures) slides in at the right edge, labelled 'fava beans'. On 'destroy', the cell's ROSE outline flickers and a thin crack line runs across it, then heals back (a teaser). Large white question across the top: 'Why can beans destroy red cells?'

Title 'The Bean and the Red Cell' fades in above the cell for 2 seconds while the question text fades out. The bean plate slides off the right edge. The TEAL glutathione loop keeps turning slowly; plasma particles drift.

scenes.tts: Here is a mature red blood cell. It has no nucleus and no mitochondria. It needs little ribose. What it needs is NADPH, and it gets it mainly from this pathway.
scenes.narration: Here is a mature red blood cell. It has no nucleus and no mitochondria. It needs little ribose. What it needs is NADPH, and it gets it mainly from this pathway.
scenes.caption: Here is a mature red blood cell. It has no nucleus and no mitochondria. It needs little ribose. What it needs is NADPH, and it gets it mainly from this pathway.
scenes.visual: The camera eases in until the cell fills about 70% of the frame height. On 'no nucleus', a GREY dashed circle labelled 'nucleus' flashes at the cell centre and a GREY cross strikes it; it fades. On 'no mitochondria', two small GREY dashed bean-shaped outlines labelled 'mitochondria' do the same. On 'little ribose', a tiny YELLOW five-tile chip labelled 'ribose' appears and shrinks to a dot. On 'NADPH', a steady PURPLE stream of dots begins from the left inside the cell. On 'this pathway', an ORANGE valve icon appears at the left edge inside the cell, labelled 'G6PD: the tap'; small YELLOW six-tile chips labelled 'G6P' flow into it and the PURPLE NADPH stream flows out of it toward the TEAL loop. Six items at most: cell, tap, NADPH stream, glutathione loop, G6P chips, label.

scenes.tts: Inside, glutathione peroxidase spends reduced glutathione to neutralize peroxides. Glutathione reductase then spends NADPH to restore it. The cycle turns as long as NADPH keeps coming.
scenes.narration: Inside, glutathione peroxidase spends reduced glutathione to neutralize peroxides. Glutathione reductase then spends NADPH to restore it. The cycle turns as long as NADPH keeps coming.
scenes.caption: Inside, glutathione peroxidase spends reduced glutathione to neutralize peroxides. Glutathione reductase then spends NADPH to restore it. The cycle turns as long as NADPH keeps coming.
scenes.visual: The TEAL loop grows to fill the right half of the cell. On 'glutathione peroxidase', a GREY label 'peroxidase' sits on the top arrow; a RED star drifts in from the plasma, meets the '2 GSH' chip and is snuffed out to a GREY puff while a TEAL token moves along the top arrow and becomes 'GSSG'. On 'Glutathione reductase', a GREY label 'reductase' sits on the bottom arrow; a PURPLE NADPH dot enters it, hands off its white electron dots, and the token returns along the bottom arrow to '2 GSH'. On 'as long as NADPH keeps coming', the loop speeds up to a steady rhythm, each turn matched by one PURPLE dot from the ORANGE tap. ROSE hemoglobin dots drift calmly in the cell.

scenes.tts: So the red cell's whole glutathione cycle leans on one enzyme. It is G six P D, the committed first step of this pathway.
scenes.narration: So the red cell's whole glutathione cycle leans on one enzyme. It is G6PD, the committed first step of this pathway.
scenes.caption: So the red cell's whole glutathione cycle leans on one enzyme. It is G6PD, the committed first step of this pathway.
scenes.visual: The guiding idea. Pull back slightly so the whole cell shows. A single bright ORANGE line traces the route: from the ORANGE tap, along the PURPLE NADPH stream, into the TEAL loop, and around it. On 'leans on one enzyme', the TEAL loop tilts gently toward the tap as if resting its weight on it. On 'G six P D', the tap brightens and its label grows to 'G6PD: first step'. White text at top: 'One enzyme carries the cycle'. The loop keeps turning.

scenes.tts: G six P D deficiency weakens that step. It is the most common human enzyme deficiency, in roughly four hundred million people. The gene sits on the X chromosome, so males are affected more often.
scenes.narration: G6PD deficiency weakens that step. It is the most common human enzyme deficiency, in roughly 400 million people. The gene sits on the X chromosome, so males are affected more often.
scenes.caption: G6PD deficiency weakens that step. It is the most common human enzyme deficiency, in roughly 400 million people. The gene sits on the X chromosome, so males are affected more often.
scenes.visual: On 'weakens that step', the ORANGE tap dims to about 40% brightness and its handle narrows; the YELLOW G6P chips queue at it and pass slowly, and the PURPLE NADPH stream thins to sparse dots. The TEAL loop slows but still turns (no trigger yet). On 'four hundred million', a large white counter at top right reads '~400 million people'. On 'X chromosome', the counter is replaced by a simple white 'X' glyph labelled 'gene on X'; then two small figure icons appear under it, one tagged 'XY' and one tagged 'XX'; the 'XY' icon glows ORANGE-dim on 'males are affected more often'. No pedigree, no percentages.

scenes.tts: Its many variants differ in severity. Then a trigger arrives: fava beans, certain antimalarial or sulfa drugs, or an infection. Each pushes oxidative stress past what a weakened cell can handle.
scenes.narration: Its many variants differ in severity. Then a trigger arrives: fava beans, certain antimalarial or sulfa drugs, or an infection. Each pushes oxidative stress past what a weakened cell can handle.
scenes.caption: Its many variants differ in severity. Then a trigger arrives: fava beans, certain antimalarial or sulfa drugs, or an infection. Each pushes oxidative stress past what a weakened cell can handle.
scenes.visual: On 'differ in severity', the dimmed ORANGE tap flickers through three brightness levels (schematic, no numbers) and settles at the dim one; the X and figure icons fade out. On 'a trigger arrives', three icons enter from the right edge in turn and line up outside the cell: the olive-brown bean plate 'fava beans', a plain white capsule 'certain drugs', and a GREY blob 'infection'. Each releases a burst of RED stars toward the cell. On 'past what a weakened cell can handle', RED stars arrive faster than the slowed TEAL loop can turn; a few RED stars get past the loop and drift among the ROSE hemoglobin dots.

scenes.tts: Less NADPH means less reduced glutathione. Reactive oxygen builds up. Hemoglobin oxidizes and clumps together. Those clumps are called Heinz bodies.
scenes.narration: Less NADPH means less reduced glutathione. Reactive oxygen builds up. Hemoglobin oxidizes and clumps together. Those clumps are called Heinz bodies.
scenes.caption: Less NADPH means less reduced glutathione. Reactive oxygen builds up. Hemoglobin oxidizes and clumps together. Those clumps are called Heinz bodies.
scenes.visual: The trigger icons shrink to a small row at the right edge. On 'Less NADPH', the PURPLE stream from the dim tap thins to an occasional dot. On 'less reduced glutathione', the '2 GSH' chip fades while the 'GSSG' chip brightens, and the TEAL loop stalls. On 'Reactive oxygen builds up', RED stars multiply inside the cell. On 'Hemoglobin oxidizes', the ROSE hemoglobin dots touched by RED stars turn dull brown-red; on 'clumps together', they drift into three dark knots inside the cell, outlined in RED (schematic). On 'Heinz bodies', the knots get one label 'Heinz bodies'.

scenes.tts: The damaged cells burst in the circulation, or the spleen pulls them out. The result is a hemolytic crisis, and a bean started it.
scenes.narration: The damaged cells burst in the circulation, or the spleen pulls them out. The result is a hemolytic crisis, and a bean started it.
scenes.caption: The damaged cells burst in the circulation, or the spleen pulls them out. The result is a hemolytic crisis, and a bean started it.
scenes.visual: The camera pulls back: the one cell shrinks to centre among four other small damaged cells (ROSE outlines with RED-outlined knots) drifting in a plasma stream left to right. On 'burst in the circulation', two of them split open and scatter ROSE dots. On 'the spleen', a GREY organ block labelled 'spleen' sits at the right edge; on 'pulls them out', two other damaged cells are drawn into it and vanish. On 'hemolytic crisis', white text across the top: 'hemolytic crisis'. On 'a bean started it', the small bean-plate icon in the corner pulses once. Our main cell remains in view, still damaged but intact, so the world carries on.

scenes.tts: Read the chain from start to finish. Weak G six P D. Less NADPH. Less reduced glutathione. More reactive oxygen. Clumped hemoglobin. Lost cells.
scenes.narration: Read the chain from start to finish. Weak G6PD. Less NADPH. Less reduced glutathione. More reactive oxygen. Clumped hemoglobin. Lost cells.
scenes.caption: Read the chain from start to finish. Weak G6PD. Less NADPH. Less reduced glutathione. More reactive oxygen. Clumped hemoglobin. Lost cells.
scenes.visual: The camera returns to the main cell at full size. The scattered pieces from the last scene fade. A row of six linked chips builds left to right across the bottom third of the frame, each lighting in the cell as it is spoken: ORANGE 'G6PD down' (the tap flickers), PURPLE 'NADPH down' (the stream thins), TEAL 'GSH down' (the 2 GSH chip dims), RED 'reactive oxygen up' (a RED star pulses), ROSE-brown 'Heinz bodies' (the knots pulse), GREY 'cells lost' (the cell outline flickers). Short arrows join them. The chain stays on screen through the next scene.

scenes.tts: Now a puzzle. A trait this dangerous affects roughly four hundred million people. What could keep it so common?
scenes.narration: Now a puzzle. A trait this dangerous affects roughly 400 million people. What could keep it so common?
scenes.caption: Now a puzzle. A trait this dangerous affects roughly 400 million people. What could keep it so common?
scenes.visual: The chain at the bottom dims to 40%. On 'roughly four hundred million', the white counter '~400 million people' returns at top right. Question card across the top in white: 'Why is it so common?' Nothing hints at the answer: no parasite, no map.
Predict pause. Hold the question card and the counter. The dimmed cell breathes slightly; plasma particles drift; a single RED star drifts slowly past. No other change.

scenes.tts: It is thought to persist because it offers some protection against malaria. Deficient red cells seem to be a poorer home for the parasite, Plasmodium falciparum. Where the trait is common broadly overlaps malaria's historical range.
scenes.narration: It is thought to persist because it offers some protection against malaria. Deficient red cells seem to be a poorer home for the parasite, Plasmodium falciparum. Where the trait is common broadly overlaps malaria's historical range.
scenes.caption: It is thought to persist because it offers some protection against malaria. Deficient red cells seem to be a poorer home for the parasite, Plasmodium falciparum. Where the trait is common broadly overlaps malaria's historical range.
scenes.visual: The question card dissolves; the chain fades out. On 'some protection against malaria', a small GREY oval with a faint inner dot, labelled 'malaria parasite' (cartoon, not a structure), drifts toward the dim-tap cell. On 'poorer home', it slips inside the cell, fails to thrive there, and fades out; a small tag 'seems' hangs beside it. On 'broadly overlaps', the cell shrinks to the left third and two large translucent rounded shapes appear at right: an ORANGE-outlined one labelled 'trait common' and a GREY-outlined one labelled 'malaria, historically'. They slide together until they mostly, but not completely, overlap. A tag under them: 'schematic, not a map'.

scenes.tts: That makes it a balanced polymorphism, like sickle-cell trait. How strong the protection is, and in whom, still differs between studies. It is also why doctors screen for it before prescribing certain oxidant drugs.
scenes.narration: That makes it a balanced polymorphism, like sickle-cell trait. How strong the protection is, and in whom, still differs between studies. It is also why doctors screen for it before prescribing certain oxidant drugs.
scenes.caption: That makes it a balanced polymorphism, like sickle-cell trait. How strong the protection is, and in whom, still differs between studies. It is also why doctors screen for it before prescribing certain oxidant drugs.
scenes.visual: The overlap shapes merge into a simple balance beam at right: left pan labelled 'risk: hemolysis' holding the small bean-plate icon, right pan labelled 'some malaria protection'. The beam rocks gently and settles level; label above: 'balanced polymorphism'. On 'still differs between studies', the beam wobbles slightly and a small tag 'debated strength' appears. On 'screen for it', the beam fades and the white capsule icon from the trigger scene reappears beside the cell with a white checklist icon labelled 'G6PD screen first'. No dosing, no drug names.

scenes.tts: So one weak step cuts both ways. It leaves a red cell exposed to a bean, and may leave it a poorer home for a parasite.
scenes.narration: So one weak step cuts both ways. It leaves a red cell exposed to a bean, and may leave it a poorer home for a parasite.
scenes.caption: So one weak step cuts both ways. It leaves a red cell exposed to a bean, and may leave it a poorer home for a parasite.
scenes.visual: The cell returns to full size, centre-left, dim ORANGE tap at its left edge. On 'cuts both ways', two thin arrows grow from the dim tap: one to the bean-plate icon at upper right (labelled 'exposed'), one to the GREY parasite icon at lower right (labelled 'poorer home?'). The parasite arrow is dashed to keep the hedge. Both icons then fade.

scenes.tts: Either way, the red cell's antioxidant shield hangs on a single step. Weaken G six P D, add an oxidant, and the whole chain gives way.
scenes.narration: Either way, the red cell's antioxidant shield hangs on a single step. Weaken G6PD, add an oxidant, and the whole chain gives way.
scenes.caption: Either way, the red cell's antioxidant shield hangs on a single step. Weaken G6PD, add an oxidant, and the whole chain gives way.
scenes.visual: The tap brightens back to full ORANGE for a moment: the PURPLE stream flows, the TEAL loop spins, RED stars are snuffed (the healthy cell). On 'Weaken G six P D', the tap dims again; on 'add an oxidant', one RED star burst arrives from the plasma; on 'the whole chain gives way', the PURPLE stream thins, the TEAL loop stalls, and the ROSE dots knot, in that order, along the same route the ORANGE line traced in s04.

End card over the dimmed but still moving red-cell world (plasma particles drifting, the TEAL loop turning slowly beside the ORANGE tap). Large centred white text: 'A red cell's antioxidant defense leans on NADPH, gated by G6PD.'
